facts.text: Director Stuart Gordon spotted a Castle Freak poster in producer Charles Band's office: a Quasimodo-like man chained to a wall. Band's pitch: "Well, that's a castle and there's a freak."
Continuity goof: the bread the Duchess carries to her prisoner has a big hole in it in the kitchen, but it's whole by the time it reaches the dungeon.
Stuart Gordon made Castle Freak for about $500,000, tiny even for Full Moon. His trade: no rating, final cut, and any cast he wanted.
The Castle Freak poster art was designed before anybody wrote the script. The screenplay was built around a picture.
Stuart Gordon first heard the pitch in winter and was shooting by June 1994. Production moved fast, and he said the castle gave the film its scale.
The castle is real and was owned by Full Moon boss Charles Band. Director Stuart Gordon had already shot The Pit and the Pendulum there four years earlier.
Drive-In Totals: Eight dead bodies. Seven breasts. One dead cat, skinned. One extended chase scene. One motor vehicle crash. Random skull paintings. Abandoned toy room. Dangling clown doll.
Jeffrey Combs (John Reilly) has starred in five movies based on H.P. Lovecraft stories. Fans call him "the first Lovecraftian actor."
The end credits give special thanks to H.P. Lovecraft and "the wonderful people of Giove, Italy," the Umbrian town where the film was shot.
In the car-crash flashback, the portable game console JJ plays with is a Sega Game Gear.
Barbara Crampton (Susan Reilly) has appeared in five H.P. Lovecraft adaptations, starting with Re-Animator (1985) and From Beyond (1986), both directed by Stuart Gordon.
Director Stuart Gordon told his crew he wanted realistic performances and a documentary feel, a deliberate contrast to the wild comic gore of his earlier Lovecraft films like Re-Animator.
Stuart Gordon shot the film handheld to save time. It adds a subtle hover that makes it feel like the creature is always watching.
Jonathan Fuller, who plays the castle freak Giorgio, lost weight for the role.
Full Moon's Paramount distribution deal collapsed during post-production. The American actors reportedly refused to record dialogue until they were paid owed overtime.
Mondo Digital calls the film one of the best in the Full Moon catalog. It credits a terrific physical performance by Jonathan Fuller and a jittery score by Richard Band.
The film is loosely based on H.P. Lovecraft's "The Outsider," about a being who leaves his dungeon and sees his own distorted body in a mirror. Gordon and writer Dennis Paoli both cited it.
The 1996 UK video release lost 1 min 9 sec to the BBFC, including a cat being dragged through a hatch, a woman's breast being bitten and mutilated female bodies.
The freak makeup took six hours to apply every day on actor Jonathan Fuller.
Composer Richard Band wrote the score mostly for strings, inspired by Bernard Herrmann, and had percussionists strike the strings with mallets for the violent moments.
Charles Band owns the castle, and the crew once had to scrub blood and guts off the floors and walls fast because a Band family reunion was about to be held there.
Screenwriter Dennis Paoli says the monster Giorgio was never meant as a zombie. He was conceived as the manifestation of familial dread and abuse.
Continuity goof: the mirror Giorgio smashes is broken differently in the next shot, when the family arrives.
Castle Freak was slated for a Halloween 1994 theatrical release. It was pushed to direct-to-video in November 1995, the first Full Moon film released outside of Paramount.
Full Moon was short on money during production. Stuart Gordon said, "I don't think there was any money to do one-sheets," so the film had no real posters, though it found its audience.
The castle is the Castello di Giove (Castle of Jupiter) in Umbria. Director Stuart Gordon knew it well, and the real setting pulled the script closer to Lovecraft's atmospheric style.
The police say the castle has more than 150 rooms. The real location gave the production plenty of room to explore.
Drive-In Totals: Chain strangling. Forehead wall-bashing. Crypt destruction. Casket cracking. Eye chewing. Spine stabbing. Whip wielding. Wine bottle bashing. Hooker shackling.
Before playing a monster, Jonathan Fuller was chosen in a nationwide search in 1984 to play Jesus Christ in The Glory of Easter at the Crystal Cathedral.
Jeffrey Combs on his character John and the creature: "The beast, the freak, and I are Yin and Yang." He called the film "cruel, graphic, but beautiful."
Jeffrey Combs (John Reilly) said of his guilt-ridden character: "I can never really release myself from the terrible things my character feels guilty about."
This is the third Stuart Gordon film in which Barbara Crampton's character bares her breasts and is groped by the monster, after Re-Animator and From Beyond.
Castle Freak was meant for a Full Moon sub-label called PulsePounders, for extreme unrated horror. The name ended up on a kids' video line instead.
Jeffrey Combs auditioned for Commander Riker on Star Trek: The Next Generation. He lost, but later played Weyoun and Brunt on Deep Space Nine and Shran on Enterprise.
The unrated director's cut has more explicit sex and gore than the R-rated version. Both were released on VHS and Laserdisc in November 1995.
Besides the unrated cut, there is an R-rated version of Castle Freak that runs about 54 seconds shorter.
Stuart Gordon was originally going to direct Lurking Fear (1994), a Full Moon Lovecraft film. Castle Freak became his Full Moon film instead.
Drive-In Totals: Eye chewing aside, the film has Chambermaid bludgeoning. Ear ripping. Chain jerking. Butcher knife to the forearm. Sexual assault by claw. Thumb rolls. Breast rolls. Eye rolls.
Barbara Crampton (Susan Reilly) said the film "preys on human weaknesses in a crude, realistic way." She was reunited with Re-Animator director Stuart Gordon and co-star Jeffrey Combs.
The film got a shout-out in the Full Moon spoof Demonic Toys: Personal Demons (2010).
Jonathan Fuller's film diary says the crew was a day and a half behind on July 7, 1994. On July 8, Charles Band arrived with his wife and father and said filming must end by July 9.
Barbara Crampton began on soap operas, debuting on Days of Our Lives in 1983. She became a horror icon through Re-Animator, From Beyond and You're Next.
Real brain matter was reportedly used for the film's gory finale.
A remake of Castle Freak, produced by Barbara Crampton and directed by Tate Steinsiek, debuted on video-on-demand on December 4, 2020.
Screenwriter Dennis Paoli says most of his script got shot, with little cut. The finale was shortened in the edit for more impact.
Barbara Crampton was meant to be fully naked in this scene. She felt the castle was too cold, so she only removed her blouse and bra.
Basic TV airings cut this scene entirely, so it's unclear how Susan lures the creature away from her daughter.
